title: Rankings, ADP and Auction Prices: What to Trust in a 9-Cat League
brief: Why are Yahoo ranks, X-rank, ADP and straight 9-cat total rankings unreliable for our H2H 9-cat league, and how do points-league values leak into our draft room? It must show how to use rank versus market price to find value and when a gap between sites is an opportunity.
summary: No single public number tells you a player's value in our 12-team H2H 9-cat auction. Yahoo X-rank, Yahoo ADP and straight 9-cat total rankings either ignore our format, mix in points-league drafts, or inflate a few players. Use format-matched rankings for value and ADP or auction data only as the market price. Act only on large gaps, and remember that some points-league favorites will cost too much in our room.

sections.heading: First question: which format is this number for?

paragraphs.text: A ranking with no format attached is useless. A player's value changes between H2H categories, roto, Yahoo points, ESPN points and Sleeper. Labels like sleeper, bust or overrated mean nothing until you know which format they come from. Before you use any list for the 2026-10-18 auction, confirm that it is built for 12-team, 9-cat, head-to-head play.

Yahoo ranks and ADPs are the same for every format. They do not change with your league settings. Yahoo's X-rank is a vibes-based expert list that ignores format and often floats somewhere between points value and category value. The Yahoo draft room sorts by X-rank by default. The separate 'rank' column comes from statistical projections and does change with league settings. In our room, sort by that 'rank' column, not by X-rank.

Rankings also differ a lot between Yahoo, ESPN and Fantrax. So whether a player is a bust or a steal depends on platform and format. ESPN's default leagues use 10 teams and 8 categories. Convert ESPN ranks before you compare them to our 12-team 9-cat format.

sections.heading: Why straight 9-cat totals mislead in H2H

paragraphs.text: Many experts say straight 9-cat total rankings are the worst way to value players. One analyst never uses them at all. The examples are extreme: by 9-cat per-game rankings Giannis ranked around 69th or 70th, and nobody believes that. If a ranking needs a 50-spot correction to reflect a player's real value, the system is wrong.

You cannot cherry-pick. If you trust one 9-cat ranking for one player, you have to accept every result it gives, including the absurd ones. If you don't believe those results, don't use the numbers for anyone.

The error goes in both directions. 'Nine-cat fluffies' are players the traditional Z-score method overrates, partly because it counts turnovers. These players get overdrafted. One-category specialists can look like top-100 players once you punt their weak categories. That does not make them draftable in a standard league like ours. In the other direction, a low 9-cat rank can wrongly suggest a useful player belongs on waivers or the bench. Paolo Banchero is the example given. Past finishes mislead too: one expert calls Turner's top-20 finish a flaw in the rankings and says Zubac's 9-cat rank did not reflect his real value.

H2H is not the same as season totals. One analyst's H2H system pushes centers down. In H2H you want to max out games played, so low turnovers matter less. He also says traditional box-score values overrate blocks, steals and some percentages. Yahoo's full-season total rankings can also reward games played too much. Reed Sheppard, with 82 games, was ranked far too high. When you check a cheap big man or a high-games player, ask whether his rank comes from real weekly impact or from the formula.

sections.heading: How points-league value leaks into our room

paragraphs.text: Yahoo ADP mixes points drafts and category drafts. So players valued for points leagues can show up high in category draft rooms and near the top of autodraft queues. Yahoo also ranks some players for category leagues and others for points leagues. Players whose Yahoo rank is boosted by one format are hard to value correctly for the other.

The usual leak is the high-usage volume scorer. Usage correlates strongly with points-league value but much less with category success. A scorer with weak defensive stats and lower efficiency can be top 10 in points leagues but only a third-rounder in category leagues. In 9-cat, efficiency, assists, steals and blocks matter more. Rule for our auction: do not pay the room's price for a player whose value is mostly points. This is not a points league.

The leak also creates bargains. Players with a big gap between their points value and their category value can be mispriced. Target the ones whose rank or ADP reflects their weaker points value, because the market is pricing them for the other format. Not every drafter knows why a player is ranked where he is, so many get fooled by bad ranks.

sections.heading: Rank versus market price: finding value

paragraphs.text: Keep two numbers apart. Format-matched rankings and projections tell you a player's quality. ADP, or auction price data, is the market price and tells you when he will likely be available. The example: if you rank a player 30th and his ADP is 70th, take him in the 50s. Translated to our auction, bid above his market price but stay below what your own 9-cat rank says he is worth. Do not open at your full value when the room will let him go cheaper.
Yahoo auction price data currently differs a lot from snake-draft ADP. Treat them separately. For our auction, use auction price data as the market price. Use snake ADP only as a rough signal.

Act only on large gaps. A gap of a few spots leaves little margin for error. A gap of 15 to 20 spots protects you even if the player underperforms. Also remember ADP is an average, not a median. A player with ADP 50 goes after pick 50 in roughly half of drafts. A player with ADP 46 goes outside the top 50 in some leagues, and others often go earlier than their number. Treat any single ADP as a range, not a fixed point.

Clean the market data before you trust a gap. A Yahoo ADP based on very few drafts can be inflated. Ignore ADPs distorted by dynasty leagues where the player is drafted in only a small share of leagues. ADPs also tend to just follow last season. Rank and ADP feed each other: when Yahoo moves a player's rank back, his ADP drifts later too. Do not wait for a site to 'fix' an ADP. ADPs are not set by a person. They update daily from real drafts, so what you see on 2026-10-18 is the current market.

The experts disagree on how much weight Yahoo's ranks deserve. One side says Yahoo is the most-used platform and its rankings drive ADP in mock and real drafts. So use them as a baseline for where players will go. Rank and ADP are the only large-scale guides to drafter behavior, but how much they matter depends on the league: some follow ranks, some follow ADP, some go rogue. The other side says format-agnostic Yahoo ranks fit no single format and should not be trusted, and that rankings without a format are useless. The working compromise for us: use Yahoo ranks to predict what our 11 opponents will bid, and never to set your own value. Watch the first nominations to see whether our room follows ranks, ADP or neither.

sections.heading: When a gap between sites is an opportunity

paragraphs.text: Learn how each site presents its data and how value differs across formats. You can gain value from the gaps. When a player's ESPN ADP is far later than his rank, drafters are passing on him round after round. Grab him when you see the same thing happen in our room. Convert ESPN's 10-team 8-cat numbers first.

Players with similar category profiles, for example rebounds, blocks and FG%, should go in about the same area. A huge ADP gap between two such players is a market inefficiency. Buy the cheaper one rather than paying up for the more famous one.

Checklist before you act on a gap. One: is your value from a 9-cat H2H source, not straight 9-cat totals or points rankings? Two: is the gap 15 to 20 spots or more? Three: is the market number clean, meaning not based on few drafts, not distorted by dynasty, and not just last season repeated? Four: is the gap explained by points-league pricing? If so, it is a buy when the player is better in categories and a pass when he is better in points.
